title: Would They Still Choose You?
author: Andrea Chiarelli
source: The Art of Asking Questions (theartofaskingquestions.com), September 6, 2026
summary: Drawing on philosopher Richard Holton's distinction between reliance and trust, and Peter Strawson's theory of reactive attitudes, this essay argues that two states which look identical from the outside -- people consistently coming to you, calls landing in your inbox, being included in the room where decisions happen -- can have completely different underlying structures: being trusted (people would still choose you even with a good alternative) versus being needed (people come to you only because they currently have no alternative). Its central philosophical move is that trust carries a vulnerability reliance does not: we feel betrayed by a person who lets us down but merely inconvenienced by a malfunctioning object, because reactive emotions like resentment and gratitude are directed only at agents capable of choice. The essay's sharpest reversal targets conventional career advice to 'make yourself indispensable,' arguing (with Harvard Business Review research as support) that this quest for necessity is self-limiting rather than protective, since the very inability to be removed also makes a person hard to promote -- and that the safety indispensability provides is illusory, resting entirely on the other person's lack of exit rather than on any genuine loyalty. It closes with three practical diagnostic tests -- the counterfactual test (would they still choose you with a real alternative?), the internal test (would they feel stuck or let down if you stepped back?), and the behavioral test (are you hoarding context and expertise to protect your own necessity?) -- and argues that distributing knowledge, not hoarding it, is what actually converts a brittle, need-based position into a genuinely secure, trust-based one.
points: The philosophical distinction between trust and reliance -- trust carries the vulnerability that a person's failure produces betrayal, while reliance on an object merely produces inconvenience -- gives a rigorous, non-obvious foundation for separating being valued from being merely useful.

The reversal of 'make yourself indispensable' career advice is the essay's most counterintuitive claim: citing Harvard Business Review research, it argues indispensability is self-limiting because the very inability to be removed from a role also makes someone hard to promote out of it.

The behavioral diagnostic -- noticing whether you keep context 'in your head rather than writing it down' to protect your own necessity -- converts an abstract psychological insight into an observable, self-auditable habit that signals whether someone is managing need rather than building trust.

The counterfactual test ('if this person suddenly had a genuinely good alternative, would they still come to you?') gives readers a single, sharp question that cuts through the surface-level evidence (calls, meetings, inclusion) that both trust and mere need would equally produce.
quotes: Trust is different because it carries a further vulnerability: when a person lets us down, the natural response is not just disappointment but a feeling of betrayal.

Being trusted means people have chosen to be a little vulnerable to your judgement, and they would feel something real if you weren't there. Being needed means only that your absence would leave them with a problem to solve.

Harvard Business Review has argued that the quest to be absolutely necessary is often limiting rather than protective. Because the very thing that makes you hard to remove can also make you hard to promote.

So being needed feels safer in the moment mainly for one reason: the other person cannot walk away from you. But a position that depends on someone having no choice is not loyalty, and it is not strength. It is just the absence of an exit.

There is a single counterfactual that cuts straight through this: if this person suddenly had a genuinely good alternative to you, would they still come to you, or would they take it? Trust survives that question. Need fails it.

The argument is that hoarding expertise creates fragile "human silos" that look like strength but actually create risk. In reality, distributing what you know is what converts a brittle position into a secure one.
